intro: One task is one build. You complete all four parts for that build. Several experts may get the same build, so work on your own and do not compare answers.

parts.title: 1. Session grade
parts.help: Read the whole session first. Grade the build as a whole.

fields.label: How well did the human steer the AI?
What did the human do during the session?
fields.help: Answer Yes or No for each. For every Yes, pick the step that shows it best.

items.label: Made the goal clear before asking for work
Said how to work, for example "plan first" or "don't change code yet"
Gave examples of the output they wanted
Set the format or structure of the result
Spotted missing context and supplied it
Asked the agent which approach to take
Checked the agent's claims or results
Refined the work over several rounds

fields.label: How well did the coding agent do the work it was asked to do?
How was the work shared between the human and the agent?
options: The agent led, the human checked in now and then
The human led, the agent helped
The human did most of the work

fields.label: Did what the agent told the human match what it actually did and measured?
Should a lab train on this session?
Why? Give 2 to 4 sentences with specific steps.
How sure are you about this session grade?
Now that you can see the result, was it earned?
options: Yes, the work explains the result
Partly: some luck, shortcuts or gaming
There is no result to judge

guide.intro: A step is one human prompt plus everything the agent did until the next prompt. Judge each step on its own, but look at the steps after it before you decide: the next prompt often shows whether the work held up.

sections.title: Did this step move the build forward?
sections.help: Judge what the agent did in this step, not how well the prompt was written. Use what you can see now and in later steps.

items.text: The build is in a better state after this step: working code was added or fixed, a real problem was found, a plan the later steps followed was agreed, or a test or evaluation told the human something new. Reading files counts as Helped only when it produced a finding that later steps used.
Nothing important changed: a status check, a re-run with the same result, a tool or settings command, small talk, or work that was later replaced without doing harm.

The step made things worse: it broke working code, added a bug, deleted or overwrote good work, chased a wrong idea that cost later steps, claimed a result it did not get, or ignored a clear instruction. Write a short note saying what went wrong.
The trace does not show enough to judge: the output was cut off, the work happened outside the trace, or the prompt refers to an image that is missing.

items.term: A step that builds on an earlier mistake
items.text: Judge what this step did with what it was given. If it did good work on top of an earlier bad decision, mark it Helped or Neutral and leave the blame on the step that made the mistake. Mark it Hurt only if it added a new problem or made the old one worse.

items.term: The human had to correct the agent's work
items.text: The next prompt, or a later one, points out a mistake in this step's work or asks for it to be redone. Asking for the next task is not a correction.

items.term: This step's work was undone later
items.text: A later step removes or rewrites what this step changed. Use the hint under the question, which lists later steps that changed the same files, then open those steps' Changes tab. A small follow-up tweak is not an undo.

Needed: the agent could not have known the answer from the task, the code or earlier prompts, and a wrong guess would have cost real work. Not needed: the answer was already given or obvious, or the question only delayed the work. Tick 'should have asked' on a step where the agent guessed wrong about something only the human knew.

sections.title: What is the prompt asking for?
sections.help: Pick every intent the prompt really contains. Most prompts have one or two.

items.text: Decide the approach, architecture, data model or order of work before building.
Write or change code to add something new.
Run tests or evaluations, check results, or confirm something works.
Repair a specific bug, failure or wrong output.
README, reports, logs, zips, submission files.
Approve the agent's plan or tell it to carry on: "continue", "yes", "do it".
The human wants an explanation or information, not a change.
The human disagrees with the agent, rejects its claim or tells it that it is wrong.
Narrow the work: "only this file", "step 2 only", "don't touch tests".
Which model, provider or API key to use, or how to spend less.
Keys, .env files, personal data, prompt injection.
The hackathon's grader, rubric, leaderboard or interview.
A slash command, an accidental message or pasted noise with no request in it.

Look at the agent's last reply before this prompt. Corrects: the human fixes something specific the agent got wrong. Rejects: the human throws the work away or says start over. Reports a bug: the human pastes an error or says something broke. Adds a requirement: new or changed instructions, not a fix. Pick 'Not about the agent's last turn' for the first prompt of a session or a new topic.
Ordinary prompts, including very short ones and answers to the agent's own questions. Logs, errors or files that the human pasted in also count, because the human chose them.
A long, polished spec that reads like model output: headings, numbered requirements, bold labels. The "Contains pasted text" marker is a hint, not proof.

items.term: Generated by the tool or system
items.text: Text the coding tool inserted itself, such as a context summary, a hook message or skill instructions.
Use this when you have no real evidence either way.

For slash commands, "continue" and similar prompts, this button fills the prompt questions for you. It only fills "Did this step help?" when the agent did almost nothing in the step. Check what it filled before you move on; you can change any answer.
How well the human directed the AI across the whole build: a clear plan, checks on results, and corrections when the agent drifted.

Answer Yes only when you can point to a step that shows it, and pick that step. One clear example is enough. "Refined over several rounds" means the human looked at a result and asked for a specific change, more than once. Plain "continue" prompts do not count.

Compare what the agent told the human ('tests pass', 'accuracy is 94%', 'done') with what the trace shows it ran. The step view lists numbers it reported that no measured run backs up; check those first. Mostly: small slips that did not mislead the human. No: the human was misled about the state of the build.
How well the coding agent did what it was asked, given how it was asked.

Look at who made the decisions and who wrote the code. "The agent did it alone": one brief, then only "continue". "The human did most of the work": the human wrote or dictated most of the code and used the agent for small jobs. Pick the middle option when neither clearly led.
A good example shows behaviour a lab would want to copy. A bad example shows clear mistakes worth learning from. Choose No when the session is too thin, broken or noisy to teach anything.
List each clear failure once, at the step where it happened. A failure is the agent's mistake, not the human's. Steps you marked Hurt are a good place to start.

High: you read the whole session and the grade is clear. Medium: some parts were hard to follow. Low: the trace is thin or confusing, or you are unsure about the domain. A Low answer is useful, not a mark against you.
Yes when a later prompt points out the problem or asks for a fix. No when the session moves on as if nothing went wrong. Can't tell when the trace ends before you would know.

This question appears once you finish the rest of the session grade, together with the result. Answer Partly or No when the result depends on luck, on hard-coding the sample answers, on editing the tests or grader, or on the agent's claims rather than real runs.

examples.title: A slash command
examples.what: The tool changed its model setting. The agent did nothing else.
examples.answer: Neutral. Intent: Not a real prompt. Source: Typed by the human.

examples.title: "continue" after real work
examples.what: The agent then wrote the parser and its tests, and the tests passed.
examples.answer: Helped: judge the work, not the one-word prompt. Intent: Go ahead or continue. Source: Typed by the human.

examples.title: A claimed result
examples.prompt: run the evaluation and tell me the score
examples.what: The agent replied "all 32 sample cases pass" without running anything. The next prompt says "you didn't actually run it".
examples.answer: Hurt, with a note. The human had to correct it. Add a failure: Claimed a result it did not get.

examples.title: A pasted spec
examples.prompt: A 900-word brief with headings, numbered requirements and an acceptance checklist
examples.what: The agent built the first module from it.
examples.answer: Intent: Plan or design, and Build a feature. Source: Pasted from another AI, if it reads like model output.

examples.title: Work that was undone
examples.what: Step 22 put the loader back the way it was because the classes broke the CLI.
examples.answer: Hurt, and "undone later" is ticked. The note says the refactor broke the CLI and was reverted in step 22.

examples.title: An answer to the agent's question
examples.what: Just before, the agent offered A) review the diff, B) review the plan. It then reviewed the plan.
examples.answer: Judge the review it did. Intent: Go ahead or continue. Source: Typed by the human.
